prompt: Match the model family to its lab: Claude, Gemini, Llama.
options: OpenAI, Meta, Google
Anthropic, Google, Meta
Google, Anthropic, Mistral
Anthropic, Meta, Google
explanation: Claude is Anthropic's model family, Gemini is Google's (DeepMind), and Llama is Meta's open-weights family. Knowing the lab tells you a lot about a model's positioning: Anthropic emphasizes safety and coding, Google leans multimodal and long-context, Meta champions open weights.
nuance: OpenAI's GPT models and xAI's Grok round out the major US frontier families; DeepSeek and Qwen (Alibaba) lead the Chinese open-weights ecosystem.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — lab landscape coverage

prompt: What does it mean for a model to be "open-weights"?
options: Its training data is fully public
The trained model weights are downloadable, so anyone can run or fine-tune it themselves — though the training data and code may stay private
It's free to use through any API
It has no usage restrictions of any kind
explanation: Open-weights means you can download and run the model yourself (Llama, DeepSeek, Mistral models). That's distinct from fully open-source — training data, code, and recipes usually remain private, and licenses may still restrict some commercial uses.
nuance: Open weights enable self-hosting for privacy, cost control at scale, and fine-tuning freedom — but you take on the infrastructure burden that API providers otherwise handle.
source_title: DeepLearning.AI — The Batch on open models

prompt: You need to classify 10 million short customer messages by sentiment, cheaply. Which class of model fits best?
options: The largest frontier reasoning model available
A small, fast, cheap model (Haiku/Flash/mini class) — the task is simple and volume is huge
An image-generation model
A fine-tuned 405B-parameter model
explanation: Simple, high-volume tasks are exactly what small models are for: sentiment classification doesn't need frontier reasoning, and at 10M calls the cost difference between a small and frontier model is often 20–60x. Match model capability to task difficulty.
nuance: A common production pattern is routing: a small model handles the easy 90% and escalates ambiguous cases to a bigger model.

prompt: You must analyze a single 500-page contract in one shot. Which model characteristic matters most?
options: Image generation quality
Context window size — the document must fit in the model's working memory
Tokens-per-second output speed
Whether the model is open-weights
explanation: A 500-page contract is roughly 250k+ tokens, so the binding constraint is context window. Models with 1M+ token windows (Gemini pioneered this class) can ingest it whole; smaller-window models would need chunking and multi-pass strategies.
nuance: Fitting isn't everything — test whether the model actually uses information from the middle of long documents well ('needle in a haystack' performance varies).

prompt: A new model tops a popular benchmark. Why should you still run your own evaluation before switching?
options: Benchmarks are always fabricated by labs
Benchmark tasks may not resemble your use case, scores can be inflated by training-data contamination, and top benchmarks saturate — small differences at the top rarely predict real-world wins
Newer models are always worse at older tasks
Benchmarks only measure speed, not quality
explanation: Benchmarks measure narrow skills, and models are sometimes inadvertently (or deliberately) trained on benchmark-like data, inflating scores. A model that wins MMLU by 1% may lose badly on your specific extraction task. Your own eval set is the only benchmark that matters for your product.
nuance: This is why experienced teams treat leaderboards as a shortlist generator, not a decision — and why 'benchmark saturation' pushed the industry toward harder, private, and task-specific evals.
source_title: The AI Daily Brief (podcast) — benchmark skepticism coverage

options: Multiple separate models vote on each answer
A model whose layers contain many specialized sub-networks, with only a few activated per token — giving big-model capability at lower inference cost
A panel of human experts labels the training data
An ensemble of models from different companies
explanation: MoE models have huge total parameter counts but route each token through only a small subset of 'experts,' so compute per token stays manageable. It's how several frontier and open models (e.g., Mixtral, DeepSeek's models) get strong capability efficiently.
nuance: This is why 'parameter count' comparisons became misleading — a 600B-parameter MoE may activate only ~37B parameters per token.

prompt: In LLM API pricing, which is typically true?
options: Input and output tokens cost the same
Output tokens usually cost several times more than input tokens, so long generations drive cost more than long prompts
You pay per API call regardless of length
Input tokens cost more than output tokens
explanation: Providers price input and output separately, and output tokens typically cost 3–5x more because generation is sequential and compute-heavy while input processing parallelizes. A cost-optimization insight: trimming verbose outputs often saves more than trimming prompts.
nuance: Prompt caching flips the input side too — cached input tokens can be ~10x cheaper, which matters hugely for agents that resend long contexts repeatedly.

prompt: What does the term "frontier model" mean?
options: A model designed for use in remote areas
A model at or near the current state of the art in general capability — the leading edge of what AI can do
Any model released in the last 6 months
A model trained on geographic data
explanation: "Frontier" refers to the capability frontier: the handful of most capable general-purpose models at any moment (recent GPT, Claude, and Gemini flagships). The term also carries regulatory weight — 'frontier labs' face the most safety scrutiny.
nuance: The frontier moves fast: today's frontier capability tends to appear in models 10–30x cheaper within about a year.

prompt: Mistral AI is best known as…
options: Google's internal model team
A French lab that made its name with strong, efficient open-weights models
A vector database company
An AI chip manufacturer
explanation: Paris-based Mistral AI became Europe's flagship AI lab by releasing compact open-weights models (Mistral 7B, Mixtral) that punched far above their size, alongside commercial API models. It's a key player in the open-weights ecosystem and European AI policy debates.
nuance: Europe's AI story is heavily tied to Mistral — it's frequently cited in EU AI Act discussions as the domestic champion.

prompt: What does it mean for a model to be "multimodal"?
options: It can run on multiple operating systems
It can process (and sometimes generate) multiple types of input — text, images, audio, video — not just text
It supports multiple languages
It has multiple context windows
explanation: Multimodal models accept mixed inputs — a screenshot plus a question, an audio clip, a video — and reason across them. Modern frontier models are natively multimodal rather than bolting a vision module onto a text model.
nuance: Output multimodality (generating images or audio, not just understanding them) is a separate capability — many models understand images but can't create them.

options: Removing toxic content from training data
Training a smaller, cheaper model to imitate a larger model's outputs, retaining much of its capability at a fraction of the cost
Deleting unused weights after training
Converting a model to run on GPUs
explanation: In distillation, a large 'teacher' model generates outputs that train a small 'student' model. It's a primary way labs make cheap, fast models that stay surprisingly capable, and it's how open-source communities bootstrap models from frontier outputs.
nuance: Distillation is also a competitive flashpoint — labs' terms of service generally prohibit using their outputs to train competing models, a rule at the center of several 2025 disputes.

prompt: When would you reach for a reasoning model (o-series, extended thinking modes) over a standard fast model?
options: For every request — reasoning models are strictly better
For genuinely hard multi-step problems — complex math, tricky debugging, intricate planning — where quality justifies extra latency and cost
For simple lookups and formatting, where speed matters
Only for image processing
explanation: Reasoning models trade time and money for depth: they can take many seconds and cost multiples more per query. That's a great trade on hard problems and a bad one for 'summarize this email.' Using them for everything burns budget and slows your product for no gain.
nuance: Many products now use hybrid approaches — models or routers that decide per-request how much thinking to apply.

prompt: True or false: Running an open-weights model yourself is always cheaper than using a hosted API.
options: True
False
explanation: False. Self-hosting means paying for GPUs (often underutilized), engineering time, and ops. Hosted APIs amortize hardware across many customers and run heavily optimized inference. Self-hosting tends to win only at sustained high volume, or when privacy/latency requirements force it.
nuance: The honest comparison is fully-loaded cost per token at your actual utilization — idle GPU hours are where self-hosting budgets die.
source_title: Lenny's Newsletter — build vs. buy in AI

prompt: What has happened to the cost of a given level of LLM capability over recent years?
options: It has stayed roughly constant
It has fallen dramatically — often 10x or more per year for equivalent capability — as models get more efficient and competition intensifies
It has risen with inflation
Costs only fall for open-weights models
explanation: The price of GPT-4-class capability collapsed within two years of its release, as smaller models matched it and providers competed. Product implication: features that are uneconomical today may be cheap next year — design with the cost curve in mind.
nuance: Andrew Ng and others argue this favors building aggressively now: prototype at today's prices, scale at tomorrow's.

prompt: Anthropic's Claude models earned a particularly strong reputation among developers in 2024–2025 for which use case?
options: Image generation
Coding and agentic software-engineering tasks
Music composition
Real-time translation
explanation: Claude models (especially the Sonnet line) became a default choice inside AI coding tools like Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and Anthropic leaned into this with Claude Code and strong scores on software-engineering benchmarks like SWE-bench.
nuance: Lab specialization is real but shifts fast — always check current comparisons rather than relying on last year's reputation.
